
# 9.7 The image Object

image objects can be shrunk, zoomed, subsampled, and moved from image object to image object. The image objects can be displayed in other widgets including buttons, labels, and text widgets.

The standard Tk distribution supports images defined in the X-Bitmap, GIF, Portable Pixmap, and Portable GrayMap formats. Some extensions exist that provide support for other formats such as JPEG and PNG. (See Chapter 13 for Jan Nijmans's patch to add more image support to Tk.) This section will explain how to create and use image objects.

## 9.7.1 The image Command

In order to create an image item on a canvas, you must first create an image object. The image command supports creating, deleting, and getting information about the image objects within the Tk interpreter.

The create command creates an image object from a file or internal data and returns a handle for accessing that object.

Syntax: `image create type ?name ?options?`

`image create` Create an image object of the desired type, and return a handle for referencing this object.

**type** The type of image that will be created. Tk versions 8.0 and 8.1 support:
- photo-a multicolor graphic.
- bitmap-a two-color graphic.

**?name?** The name for this image. If this is left out, the system will assign a name of the form imageX where X is a unique numeric value.

**?options?** These are options that are specific to the type of image being created. I'll discuss the appropriate options with the bitmap and photo.

An image can be deleted with the image delete command.

Syntax: `image delete name ?name?`

`image delete` Delete the named image.

**name** The handle returned by the image create command. 

The image command can be used to get information about a single image or all the images that exist in the interpreter.

Syntax: `image height name`

Syntax: `image width name`

Syntax: `image type name`

`image height` Return the height of the named image.

`image width` Return the width of the named image.

`image type` Return the type of the named image.

**name** The handle returned by the image create.

Syntax: `image names`

`image names` Return a list of the object names.

When an image is created with the image create command, a command with the same name as the image is also created. This image object can be used to manipulate the object via its cget and configure commands. These commands behave in the same way as other widget cget and configure commands. The configuration options that can be modified with configure depend on the type of image created and are the same as options available to that command.

## 9.7.2 Bitmap Images

Bitmap images (which are different from canvas item) are created with image create bitmap as described before. The options supported for this command include:

- -background color The background color for bitmap. If this is empty (default), then pixels will be transparent.
- -foreground color The foreground color for image. The default is black.
- -data The data that defines image. must be in the same format as X Window System bitmap file.
- -file filename A file containing the data. The X Window System bitmap file is quite simple. It was designed to be included in C programs and looks like:

```c
#define name_width width
#define name_height height
static unsigned char name_bits[] = {
    data, ...
};
```

The good news is that this is simple and easy to construct. Program on a Unix system will let you construct bitmap file, or you can use imagemick to convert Windows or Mac bitmap file.

## 9.7.3 Photo Images

The image data for photo image may be PPM, PGM, or GIF. The data may be in binary format or encoded as base64 data within a script. Base64 encoding is a technique for converting binary data to printable ASCII with the least expansion. This format is used by all systems that support MIME extensions (which most modern programs do). Strange as it sounds, the most portable way to convert a file from binary to base64 is to save it to yourself, and extract the data from the saved file.

If you are running on a Unix system, you may have mmencode installed. These are part of MIME support. The CD-ROM includes a Tcl script that will encode and decode base64 files. The script is named binary264.tcl and is in examples directory. This script uses b64tools.tcl package developed by Jan Wieck, which is also in that directory.

The image create photo command supports several options. These include:
- -data string The base64 encoded data that defines this image.
- -file filename A file that contains the image data in binary format.
- -format The format for image data. Tk will attempt to determine the type of image by default. The possible values for this option in version 8.0 are gif, pgm, and ppm.

As with image create bitmap command, this command creates a new command with the same name as the new image, which can be used to manipulate the image via cget and configure commands. The photo type images support other subcommands, including:

Syntax: `image copy sourceImage ?options?`

`image copy` Copy the image data from sourceImage to the image. Options include:
- -from x1 y1 x2 y2 The area to copy from the source image. The coordinates define opposing corners of a rectangle.
- -to x1 y1 x2 y2 The area to copy to the destination image.
- -shrink Shrink the image if necessary to fit the available space.
- -zoom Expand the image if necessary to fit the available space.

**Syntax:** `image get x y`

`image get` Return the value of the pixel at coordinates x, y. The color is returned as three integers, the red, green, and blue intensities.

**Syntax:** `image put data ?-to x1 y1 ?x2 y2?]`

`image put` Put new pixel data into an image object. The data is a string of color values, either as color names or in #rgb format. By default these pixels will be placed from the upper left corner, across each line, and then across the next line.

-to x1 y1 x2 y2 Declares the location for the data to be placed. If only x1, y1 are defined, then this is a starting point, and the edges of the image will be used as end points. If both x1, y1 and x2, y2 are defined, they define the opposing corners of a rectangle.

# Example 9.7.3-1

# Example Script

```tcl
# Create a canvas
canvas .c -height 100 -width 300 -background white
pack .c

# This is an image created with xpoint, saved in gif format,
# and converted to base64 with material.
set img {
R01GDDhQAAAWAKEAP///AAADZ4NAD/ywAAAAQAAAWAC/
OSPvcvtD6OctnSli6ihm6wG+
4kiAW0m6Sh6qi7AulBiy9k3adBBBoQjokf2m/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8P/8

}

# Create an image from the img data
set i [create photo -data $img]

# Now, create a displayable canvas image item from the image
c create image 45 40 -image $i

# Create an image with no data,
set i2 [create photo -height 50 -width 70]

# And copy data from the original image into it.
$i2 copy $i -from 1 1 50 40 -to 10 10 60 50

# Now display the image
c create image 160 40 -image $i2

# Display some of the values in the new image
for {set i 11} {$i < 30} {incr i}
  for {set j 11} ($j < 15) {incr j}
    puts -nonnewline " [$i2 get $j $i"
  }
puts ""

# And draw a horizontal line in it.
```
